newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Governor bids Hong Kong a musical farewell.
newsitem.headline: Governor bids Hong Kong a musical farewell.

text.p: Hong Kong's Governor Chris Patten bid a nostalgic musical farewell to the territory on Sunday, the eve of its handover from Britain to China, hosting a radio show on which he played some of his favourite selections.
Calling music "a crucial part of my life-support system", Patten chose music by Handel, Haydn, Mozart and Strauss among others during the hour-long programme.
But the composer who featured most prominently in his selections was Elgar, whose elegaic music is associated in many people's minds with Edwardian England and the end of empire.
Patten also recalled with fondness a group of mostly elderly Chinese musicians from Yunan who had performed at Government House.
He played the wedding piece, "Little White Plum", which they had played for him, and the sound of its Chinese cymbals and pitched reeds contrasted sharply with his other, Western selections.
Patten said the musical highlight of his five-year stay in Hong Kong had been the visit and performance of Mstislav Rostropovich, whom he termed "a genius".
He recalled that the Azerbaijani cellist was stranded for almost two hours at Hong Kong's Kai Tak airport after immigration officers apparently confused the word "cellist" with "terrorist".
Also among Patten's selections was "Highland Cathedral", played by the Royal Hong Kong Police bagpipers.

Patten's musical farewell concluded with the first of Strauss's Four Last Songs, sung by Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, including the lyric: "Now you lie in glitter and array, bathed in light like a miracle before me."

The governor commented: "Not a bad way of remembering Hong Kong as we depart in (the royal yacht) Britannia down the great lit-up bowl of the harbour in the early hours of the morning of the first of July."
Hong Kong reverts from Britain to China at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday after a colonial interlude of 156 years.
Patten's A Musical Farewell was broadcast on Sunday by Hong Kong's Radio 4 but was recorded earlier in June.
